dct_description_sm: The dietary transition from a traditional to an imported, market-based diet currently occurring in Canada's North can be problematic from a nutritional and cultural point of view. As contaminant-related dietary consumption advisories may influence food item choices and preparation methods, it is critical for these advisories to be based on the best available science and to strike a balance between the desires to reduce contaminant exposure and to maximize the nutritional and cultural value of food. The proposed work will allow for a quantitative assessment of the efficacy of such guidelines in reducing contaminant exposure. In fact, models of human dietary POP and mercury uptake/exposure, comprehensively evaluated with existing biomonitoring datasets, together with analytical consideration of food preparation impacts on contaminant bioavailability, may eventually be used to design dietary guidelines that are effective in reducing contaminant exposure, without compromising the consumption of nutritionally beneficial traditional food items.
